doc.title: Candido Camero — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Tango and jazz on Cuban radio
summary: Carlos Gardel was hugely popular, Cuban music dominated radio, and a station mixed Cuban music and jazz for jazz-loving musicians.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: You say that your uncle was fond of tango?
Was much tango listened to in Cuba at that time?
Yes, yes, yes. Carlos Gardel was very famous then, very famous, very famous. I still have several records of his. He was number one, the number one tango singer.

Because there was the impression that at that time that Cuban music was heard mostly or exclusively . . . I'm not sure if that was the situation in Cuba, that to some extent countries protected their national music ...
. . . and not much outside influence was allowed.

Well, what always predominated of course was Cuban music all over the radio, always. There was still no TV and this and that, but the radio, definitely. And all the orchestras and all septets were of Cuban music - son, danzon, guajira, guaracha, mambo, danza, contradanza, guaguancó, all this is Cuban music.
Other than the tango, what other foreign music was listened to at that time in Cuba?

A lot of American bands were heard. The musicians who liked jazz listened a lot. And there was always a station that was half Cuban music and half jazz and that was very popular among the musicians who liked jazz. So everyone was pleased with Cuban music and jazz.
